episode: LIVE: Jensen Huang on Building the Dynamo of the Intelligence Age
what: Huang describes a fundamental shift in computing from retrieval to generation, with NVIDIA's AI factories as the new dynamos. He outlines the five layers of AI investment and debunks fears of AI-driven job loss.
why: This is a foundational narrative on how AI will power the next economic era — from energy to applications. Huang's framing of AI as the third cocooning force (after electricity and the internet) is strategic.

### Chunk 1
- **Agentic AI at Google**:  
  - Sundar described the "agentic Gemini era" at Google I/O.  
  - Agentic AI refers to systems that take action on behalf of users, not just respond to queries.  
  - The "anti-gravity agent harness" is the new through line across Google products, replacing Gemini as the central framework.  
  - Anti-gravity includes an IDE, web agent experience, CLI, SDK — forming an ecosystem for developers.  
  - The same agent harness is being integrated into Google Search, Gemini app, Cloud, and Studio.

- **Agent Harness vs. Coding Harness**:  
  - Not fully synonymous; agent harness is the general framework, coding harness is a specialized use case.  
  - Specializations exist for different product needs (e.g., Data Studio for coding, Gemini app for 24/7 consumer agents).  
  - Base harness shares ~80% of functionality, with tailored optimizations for specific use cases.

- **Cannibalization Concerns**:  
  - DJ raised concerns about reduced human engagement (e.g., email) due to agentic automation.  
  - Logan countered with historical precedent: AI-enhanced search led to *more* usage, not less.  
  - Agents are also users of Google products (e.g., agents perform searches), creating new demand.  
  - Google’s long-term goal is maximizing user outcomes, not eyeball time.

- **Second-hand Agent-led Growth**:  
  - Logan coined the term to describe value creation via agents acting on behalf of users (e.g., infrastructure decisions in coding).  
  - This trend may extend beyond coding (e.g., shopping), affecting advertising and value capture models.  
  - Predicted shift is less radical than expected, with new paradigms (e.g., generative engine optimization) building on existing ones.

- **Current State of Agentic Integration**:  
  - Logan assessed Google products as being at the "crawl" stage of agentic maturity.  
  - Labs and experimental products are further along, closer to "walk" or "run."  
  - Scaling agentic features across 13B+ user products presents inherent tension and complexity.

### Chunk 3
- **Speaker: DeepMind engineer (likely Jeff Dean or similar):**
  - Uses all models (Gemini, others) internally to understand ecosystem and provide feedback.
  - Google has 100,000+ engineers using Gemini models, creating a feedback flywheel that should be a competitive advantage.
  - Gemini is the daily driver for most, but cross-model usage is encouraged for broader perspective.

- **Product acceleration via AI:**
  - Google teams are shipping products faster using AI-assisted coding (e.g., Gemini macOS app built faster than any previous Google Mac app).
  - "Anti-gravity" tools (AI coding) enable faster mobile app development.
  - AI coding is described as a "narrow super intelligence" — particularly effective at code generation.

- **On Narrow Super Intelligence (NSI):**
  - Coding is so effective it "feels like narrow super intelligence."
  - NSI in coding hasn’t displaced human developers; instead, it’s an accelerant — increasing developer agency and ambition.
  - Developers now feel capable of tackling more complex, previously out-of-reach projects.

- **Future NSI domains:**
  - Likely next domains: math, finance, science — areas with high verifiability.
  - Science is highlighted as a potentially transformative area for AI impact.
  - Desire to sequence impactful, positive AI applications early to demonstrate value.

- **AI and game development:**
  - Prediction from 2023: "Everyone will be able to vibe code video games by end of 2025" — feels close but not fully realized.
  - Not yet capable of AAA game development (e.g., Call of Duty, GTA), but accessible game creation is within reach.
  - Requires orchestration layers, tooling, and assets (e.g., sprite generation, 3D models) beyond current model capabilities.
  - AI Studio saw early surge in game development (~20% of apps), though finance and productivity now more dominant.

- **AGI vs. current capabilities:**
  - Caution against overemphasizing AGI at the expense of current transformative capabilities.
  - Current systems are already superhuman in narrow domains and should be celebrated as such.
  - AGI pursuit should not detract from maximizing the utility of current AI systems.

- **Game development as AGI benchmark:**
  - Google’s GDM team uses games as a proxy for AGI progress via the “Game Arena.”
  - Games are a deeply rooted benchmark in GDM’s history for evaluating agent capabilities.

- **Prediction for general game creation:**
  - Believes a non-expert with a good idea could create a fun, playable game using AI tools in 2025.
  - Model capability is there; product scaffolding and tooling are the current bottlenecks.

### Chunk 4
- **Startups in the AI ecosystem**:  
  - There's no significant gap in model quality, but rather in understanding how to build great games (e.g., proper scaffolding).  
  - Some startups are already doing this right, but there's a discoverability and awareness problem.  
  - Certain model capabilities are only weeks or months away from crossing the chasm to mainstream usability.

- **World models vs. coding agents for game development**:  
  - Short-term: Vibe-coded games are more likely to be powered by **coding agents + game engines**, not world models.  
  - Long-term: World models may become viable for games in ~2 years.  
  - Current world models are not well-suited for games due to open-endedness and lack of grounding in specific use cases.  
  - Startups are exploring scaffolding to make world models usable in practical contexts like gaming.

- **World model definitions are blurry**:  
  - **Omni** (Google's multimodal model) is an example of this blurriness — it’s being framed as a world model due to its deep understanding of the world.  
  - Omni differs architecturally from traditional world models like Genie, which were action-conditioned video models.  
  - Traditional world models were not scalable; Omni is more scalable and functional, though not yet real-time.  
  - The line between world models and video models is becoming less clear — Omni can perform similar visual tasks as traditional world models.

- **Omni's architecture and capabilities**:  
  - Omni is a **single model**, not a routing system across multiple models.  
  - Previously, Google used multiple models (e.g., Gemini for text, Lyria for music, etc.).  
  - Omni Flash is the first iteration; more powerful versions are in development.  
  - Current public use case: **video editing** (e.g., real-time editing of a talk with a dog entering the stage, including realistic reactions from attendees).  
  - Omni preserves the original person (e.g., speaker’s words, voice, image), but enhances the surrounding context (e.g., set design, editing).

- **AI Studio and Android app development**:  
  - AI Studio allows users to **vibe-code Android apps**, lowering the barrier to entry.  
  - Strategic goal: Integrate more Google products into AI Studio to reduce the need for multiple UIs.  
  - Example: A non-developer built a **gardening app** in AI Studio.  
  - Early feedback suggests it’s accelerating app development, though breakout hits have not yet emerged publicly.

### Chunk 5
- **350,000 Android apps** built in AI Studios since last week; many are personal-use apps, indicating a shift toward individualized AI software development.  
- **GenUI** may be farther out, but building personal-use software to solve individual problems is already happening at scale.  
- Android is becoming a **platform for AI builders**, especially with access to native phone capabilities and contextual data.  
- **Web vs. apps**: Web is powerful, but native OS features (e.g., richer text messaging experiences) offer capabilities that web-only AI chat apps currently lack.  
- **Model eats the scaffolding**:  
  - What was once considered the "model" (e.g., Gemini, GPT) is now a broader system including tool calling, code execution, agent harnesses, etc.  
  - Over time, scaffolding (e.g., agent harnesses, external tools) gets **integrated into the model** natively.  
  - Example: Agent harnesses are currently where alpha is, but likely to be absorbed into models within 12 months.  
- **Counterpoint on harness lock-in**:  
  - Startups build their own harnesses to avoid vendor lock-in.  
  - As model capabilities improve, the need for custom harnesses may diminish if models can natively support multiple harnesses.  
  - Suggestion: Need for a **"harness bench"** to measure how well models adapt to different harnesses.  
- **Application layer survival strategy**:  
  - Despite models eating scaffolding, startups can still thrive via **domain expertise**, vertical focus, and risk-taking.  
  - Startups have **agility and focus**, allowing them to outpace generalist model companies in niche areas.  
  - **Coding and agentic primitives** open new product categories and reduce barriers to entry.  
- **Google DeepMind culture**:  
  - Strong portfolio approach with broad investments; sometimes lags in specific domains due to lack of focus.  
  - Culture reflects **scientific rigor** and problem-solving ethos, influenced by Demis Hassabis and the original DeepMind team.  
  - Resembles the "Thinking Machines" documentary culture: smart people solving hard problems collaboratively.  
  - Contrasts with other labs like OpenAI (business-focused under Sam Altman) or Anthropic (esoteric, principled under Dario Amodei).

### Chunk 6
- Demis’s mission with DeepMind was to solve real-world problems like disease, not just compete on benchmarks.  
- Speaker reflects on how easy it is to lose sight of the “why” behind the work amid competitive races to push metrics higher.  
- Quote referenced: “We can’t let other people make the world a better place more than we can.”  
- Speaker finds it absurd that the tech world frames progress as a zero-sum game over who improves the world more.  
- DeepMind is described as the “engine room” of Google; this is now part of DeepMind’s Twitter/X bio.  
- DeepMind operates with a strong research (lab) culture but also collaborates widely across Google (e.g., Android, Cloud, Gmail, Workspace).  
- Deploying Gemini to billion-user products is a rare challenge, only faced by a handful of companies globally.  
- Google has 13 products with over a billion users, making it a unique environment for applied AI innovation.  
- Speaker appreciates Google’s marketing and comms teams for protecting the company’s image and narrative.  
- Speaker values the freedom to communicate authentically with developers without heavy tweet/approval processes.  
- Acknowledges the challenge large companies face in telling authentic, cohesive stories due to internal complexity.  
- Believes it’s a privilege to help Google tell its story in a more human, compelling way.  
- Praises Logan’s contributions and the human touch he and Josh bring to AI development.  
- Final takeaway: The conversation covered agents, coding, world models, benchmarks, and DeepMind-Google culture.

page_text: Anthropic’s Safety Superpower – Stratechery by Ben Thompson Skip to content Anthropic’s Safety Superpower Monday, June 15, 2026 Listen to Podcast Listen to this post : Log in to listen I’m sympathetic to the cynics who consistently characterize Anthropic’s public statements, particularly those surrounding their model releases, as scare-mongering for the sake of marketing. It was only two months ago that Anthropic announced Mythos Preview, a model that they said was too dangerous to make publicly available, thanks in particular to its advanced cybersecurity capabilities. Then, two months later, the company publicly released Fable, a version of Mythos with various safety guardrails. Fable is, in my limited experience, a very impressive model. It’s increasingly difficult to objectively evaluate models for anything other than coding performance, but there is subjective feel, and I found my interactions with Fable to be extremely impressive; it made other models, including GPT 5.5 and Opus 4.8, feel small and dumb. The two times I felt that way previously were with GPT-4 and Grok 4, both of which represented new generations in terms of base model size and complexity; my sense is that Fable is downstream of a new pre-train and the first of a new generation. To that end, I can certainly buy the case that Fable/Mythos is in fact more capable when it comes to identifying and exploiting security issues, and that Anthropic’s cautious roll-out was justified. The problem with publicly releasing models, however, is that guardrails can be jailbroken, and apparently that is exactly what happened shortly after the release. Anthropic vs. the U.S. Government, Again What happened next is somewhat unclear. Anthropic wrote in a blog post : The US government, citing national security authorities, has issued an export control directive to suspend all access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 by any foreign national, whether inside or outside the United States, including foreign national Anthropic employees. The net effect of this order is that we must abruptly disable Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all our customers to ensure compliance. Access to all other Anthropic models will not be affected. We received the directive from the government today at 5:21pm (ET). The letter did not provide specific details of its national security concern. Our understanding is that the government believes it has become aware of a method of bypassing, or “jailbreaking” Fable 5. We reviewed a demonstration of this specific technique being used to identify a small number of previously known, minor vulnerabilities. These vulnerabilities all appear relatively simple, and we have found that other publicly-available models are able to discover them as well without requiring a bypass. Anthropic went on to make the case that non-universal jailbreaks were inevitable and also narrow, and that there was no evidence of a universal jailbreak; the jailbreak that was found, meanwhile, appears to have been reported by Amazon , which is notable given Amazon is both an investor in Anthropic and a major provider of inference to the company. As I write this, senior Anthropic staff are in Washington D.C. seeking to resolve what they insist is a misunderstanding, and which White House officials are suggesting is insouciance by the company’s leadership to legitimate national security concerns. I don’t actually have much to add to the current conflict given how many facts are in dispute; what I am not surprised about is the fact that the conflict is happening: I already explained in Anthropic and Alignment why conflict between the U.S. government and Anthropic was inevitable. To that end, people who are arguing that Mythos isn’t powerful enough to warrant the government’s drastic action are missing the point: if it’s not powerful enough now, the next one will be, or the one after that, particularly now that models are increasingly useful in creating their successors. That, however, raises another question — one that seems to validate the cynics’ viewpoint: if Mythos is so dangerous, why even release Fable in the first place, and why fight with the government doing exactly what you claim to want? In fact, I think that Anthropic’s actions are quite understandable; what makes the company unique is how it justifies them, and it is those justifications that both give the cynics their fuel and Anthropic its magic. The Economic Imperative For the first few years of AI the most economic value has flown to compute, for obvious reasons: we don’t have enough supply to meet demand, which has meant skyrocketing prices; the biggest beneficiaries have been Nvidia, TSMC, and the memory makers (SK hynix, Samsung, and Micron). Anthropic and OpenAI, meanwhile, have collectively lost tens of billions of dollars building leading-edge models that, once released, are distilled and commoditized by open source models, primarily from China. This represents the bear case for the labs — they never cover their costs because their differentiation is fleeting, while free alternatives become “good enough” — and I think it’s a legitimate one. A world where models are interchangeable is one where models are commodities, while most of the value flows elsewhere. Right now that’s compute, but in the fullness of time, whenever we have enough compute, the most valuable place to be in the value chain will be the place that has always been the most valuable: owning the user touchpoint. To that end, it has long been clear to me that the frontier labs have the economic imperative to move closer to the user. If you own the user touchpoint, then you have meaningful lock-in, and the best way to own the user touchpoint is to be the canvas for everything they need to do. This, by extension, means that the frontier labs are on a collision course with software companies: it’s software that owns the user touchpoint, and it’s in the frontier labs’ long-term interest to not simply be a commodity input into software but to simply replace software outright. Software companies, meanwhile, are working to do the opposite. Satya Nadella laid out his vision for how companies should build on models in an essay on X : Every company is going to have to build what I think of as human capital and token capital. Human capital comprises the knowledge, judgment, relationships, ingenuity, and pattern recognition of its people, while token capital is the firm’s AI capability it builds and owns. Importantly, human capital does not become less valuable as token capital grows. It only becomes more valuable! I believe human agency will be the driver of token capital growth. Humans will set ambitious goals, connect dots across domains, build relationships, and recognize patterns that matter most. Without human direction, you have compute running in circles.
